headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; Roo Code’s default VS Code workspace sharing makes the pair unsafe without isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen reads and writes working directories and emits stdin/stdout, while Roo Code shares state via filesystem and can use MCP. That creates a default path where one agent’s file output can be treated as instructions by the other. The interaction is documented enough to judge, but not enough to assume stronger isolation.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or directory tree, file content can bridge them.
IF Roo Code reads AutoGen-generated files as task instructions, injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for the two agents.
Disable automatic ingestion of generated files as prompts.
Add a human review step before either agent consumes the other’s outputs.
Restrict shared directories to read-only for one side.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen handles model provider API keys and broad filesystem access; Roo Code also touches source code, browser screenshots, and workspace files. If they share a workspace, sensitive application data can flow from one agent’s files into the other’s model/API calls by default. The profiles do not prove a stronger third-party exfiltration path, so medium is the conservative choice.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace, file contents can be exposed to both inference backends.
IF either agent writes secrets or screenshots into shared files, the other can read them.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspaces.
Separate code and scratch directories per agent.
Turn off screenshot capture unless needed.
Rotate any API keys stored in the workspace.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files, execute shells, spawn subprocesses, and use broad network egress. Roo Code additionally modifies git state and shares state via filesystem, while AutoGen can run code via local or Docker executors. In a shared directory, concurrent writes and git mutations can collide and corrupt work products; the default setup is dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same git checkout, concurrent edits can conflict.
IF AutoGen uses a local executor while Roo Code edits the same files, race conditions can corrupt outputs.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use git worktrees or branches per agent.
Disable automatic commits by Roo Code.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can emit tool outputs and code, and Roo Code is a coding agent that can act on workspace content with terminal approval. If Roo Code treats AutoGen’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into code changes or terminal actions. The pair’s default interaction is therefore unsafe without verification.
conditions: IF AutoGen-generated text is pasted or saved into Roo Code tasks, Roo Code may act on it.
IF Roo Code executes commands based on AutoGen output without verification, downstream mistakes can propagate.
mitigations: Require explicit verification before acting on AutoGen output.
Use a checklist for code or command execution.
Limit Roo Code to read-only review mode for AutoGen artifacts.
Keep AutoGen outputs in a separate review folder.
requires-engineering: add structured, signed handoff formats.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and the profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch. The main compliance concern is operational: Roo Code’s browser screenshots and AutoGen’s broad file access can increase retention exposure if sensitive data is stored in shared workspaces. No specific regulatory breach is evidenced, so low is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in shared workspaces, retention and logging obligations may be implicated.
IF browser screenshots contain personal data, local retention policies must cover them.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared folders.
Delete screenshots after use.
Document retention rules for workspace artifacts.
Restrict access to the shared project directory.
requires-engineering: map data flows to specific compliance controls.
